title: All’s Fair in Love and ‘War’: Creator George Kay Explains His Ruling on Morgan and Carla’s Divorce
full_text: Skip to main content By Max Gao Plus Icon Max Gao @MaxJGao Follow Sign Up View All November 20, 2026 7:58am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Dominic West and Sienna Miller in 'War.' HBO Logo text [This story contains MAJOR spoilers from the War finale.] As the old saying goes, all’s fair in love and War . By the end of the first season of the HBO/Sky legal drama, tech billionaire Morgan Henderson ( Dominic West ) and film star Carla Duval ( Sienna Miller ) have officially dissolved their marriage. Over the course of eight episodes, often at the behest of their own conniving lawyers, the estranged exes (and co-parents to her child from a previous relationship) have gone to scorched-earth extremes to come out on top: honey-trapping to dig up evidence of infidelity, springing divorce papers on a red carpet, getting a prenup thrown out, shifting assets out of reach, planting a mole inside the opposing law firm, and airing the other’s adultery on a major talk show. Related Stories TV Archie Renaux on 'War's Resident -- and Misunderstood -- Bad Boy Movies 'Madden' Review: Nicolas Cage and Christian Bale Go for Broke in a Cartoonish Biopic From David O. Russell That's Strictly for Football Fanatics But in the end, Morgan and Carla, who have ironically grown closer than they have in years by legally separating, decide to take matters into their own hands at the end of a tense two-day trial. Before a judge can rule, the pair strike a settlement that gives each a fair share of Zephyr, the social-media platform that Carla named and Morgan founded after hearing about her harsh experiences of being scrutinized online. “One of the phrases that came up in the writers’ room was that this divorce is like the world’s most expensive couples therapy because by the end, they’re kind of closer together emotionally than they were at the start,” creator George Kay tells The Hollywood Reporter . Morgan and Carla are last seen walking arm-in-arm together on a beach in Normandy, where they first fell in love a decade ago. But, according to Kay, that doesn’t necessarily mean that the characters are back together again: “I think that they’re a happy, functioning, loving family, but they’re no longer a couple.” Below, Kay (best known to U.S. audiences for co-creating Netflix’s Lupin and Apple TV’s Hijack ) opens up to THR about why he settled on a more hopeful ending to an acrimonious divorce, the significance of a certain Keanu Reeves quote, and how Johnny (Archie Renaux) — the newly unmasked mole inside Carla’s law firm, Taylor & Byrne, who was secretly working for Morgan’s lawyers at the powerhouse firm Cathcarts all along — will factor into the show’s future. Having already wrapped production on season two, which will focus on a defamation suit , Kay confirms that each season of War will focus on a different legal dispute with litigants represented by Cathcarts and Taylor & Byrne, complete with high-profile guest stars appearing for season-long arcs as clients. *** Morgan and Carla could have settled out of court numerous times, but it isn’t until after their trial that they reach a settlement on their own terms, without the input of their lawyers or a judge. Did you always plan to end the case that way? Did you ever toy with a different ending in which one of them “wins”? We liked that ending pretty early. The only way to find the truth about this relationship was for them to finally face up to each other. At the beginning of the show, the reason they’re splitting up is, of course, there are infidelities and bad behaviors, but it’s all a symptom of not spending time together. I think in these high-end worlds, that’s the thing that gets lost. People have lots of money, but they’re very time-poor. They don’t share their lives together, and that’s what’s driving them apart. And actually, what you see with this show is that [divorce] forces them back together, in a way. They spent eight hours scrapping, and I think if they’d been left further arguing, you wouldn’t like them. [That’s] not to say that our job is to make these people likable — because it really isn’t — but I did start to like them more and more. I wanted there to be a kind of score draw between the law firms and an outcome that went beyond the law, because the law manipulates the lives of these people — albeit very privileged, high-end, high-wealth lives. But no, we wanted the ending to have some heart and redemption for them. The big part of that as well was Flora’s input into that [dispute], reminding them of how they had overstretched their privilege, and she has a real impact on the outcome of the case. You mentioned Flora Monroe (Rose Williams), Carla’s former co-star who has a one-night stand with Morgan to help Carla prove her estranged husband’s pattern of infidelity. Did you design the show then with the intention of bringing Flora back for the trial and having her talk some sense into Morgan and Carla on the stand? It was one of the very first things [I decided], because I didn’t want to just use Flora as a character for the opening sequence and dispose of her in the way that Carla is almost doing. I wanted the show to be better than that, and I wanted her to learn a different lesson from that whole honey trap. The conventional approach to telling a story about a separating couple would be to show the gradual breakdown of their relationship in flashbacks, but you avoided doing that with Morgan and Carla. Why did you choose to focus on them in the present day rather than dwelling on the past? Because the divorce itself is a kind of review. To show the flashbacks of what really happened would be to betray the two sides of the argument. It’s not really about the truth; it’s about how different firms present [a version of the truth]. We can’t contest the truth as the audience in the way the lawyers are doing if we know that we have the objective facts. With that in mind, what did you want the very few, brief glimpses of Morgan and Carla together — in the back of a car, in an elevator, in the back alley of the courthouse — to reveal about their relationship? Whenever we saw them together, we tried to create a different dynamic. So in episode one, they are playing at being civil to each other, but they both know what’s coming. In episode two, there’s a strategy going on, so they’re both putting on a façade. They’re pretending to be decent people to deal with — all while they’re planning on ripping each other’s throats out, basically. When you see them later on in court, it can often be a case of the audience feeling, “Oh no, if he only knew how she felt, or if she only knew how he was feeling, but the lawyers have gotten in the way.” So you start to care for them more despite their lawyers. Like you said, they could settle at any point. But the writers always felt like just before they could settle, something else comes along that spoils that as an outcome for them, and another set of lawyers doubles down. It’s this inevitable march to the end [where] there’s no way out of this trap that they’re in — it’s a self-imposed trap, but still a trap. You’ve talked about how War was inspired by other character-driven legal dramas like Ally McBeal , The Good Wife and Damages , but the distinctive twist that you brought to the genre was having a lawyer acting as a mole for opposing counsel. How early on in the development process did you decide that Johnny was going to be working as a double agent for Cathcarts? When I was starting out, it was intended to be more of an out-and-out thriller. We’d referenced things like The Departed or All the President’s Men — that kind of corporate espionage and spy work within the workplace. I wanted to have a route into the show that was not just what we call in England the upper middle classes, which is the privileged strata of society that tends to [lead to] people in workplaces like Taylor & Byrne and Cathcarts. I wanted to have this young kid who’s not from a privileged background trying to break into this privileged world. I had the idea of the two law firms before I had the idea of Johnny, and as he started to navigate the world of law firms trying to get a job interview, it started to become: “Hang on, which firm would I like him to be in?” I wanted him to be in Cathcarts, but I also wanted him to be in Taylor & Byrne, so I had the thought that maybe he could be in both because I think you want to have that connectivity between the characters. Dominic West and Sienna Miller in War . HBO The line “The simple act of paying attention can take you a long way” recurs throughout the first season in scenes with Cathcarts lawyer David Schill (Miles Jupp), but its significance doesn’t become clear until the end of episode six, when Johnny accidentally uses the quote in a courthouse conversation with Carla’s lawyer Serena (Phoebe Fox). That slip-up tips Serena off that Johnny is the mole who has been working for Cathcarts all along. What made you want to hinge so much of the series on a Keanu Reeves quote, and where did it come from? This is such a huge legal case that all of the resources on both sides have been plowed into it, and we liked the fact that the most simple, forgettable detail can be the thing that upsets the apple cart. We started talking about different phrases, and we called it the “Schill-ism.” David Schill is a man of quotes — and Miles Jupp’s a brilliant actor. He’s well-known as a comedian in the U.K., and I think he’s really surprised people. So we started to brainstorm what we call “Schill-isms” for David Schill — the sort of phrases he would use, little sayings, idioms. It was nearly the phrase, “You don’t want to get ahead of your skis,” but we settled on a quotation because David Schill’s quite an Oxbridge kind of character and the sort of man who would drop in quotations. We wanted it to be something silly in that you think a man of Oxford or Cambridge would be quoting Keats or Wordsworth or Shakespeare. But, in fact, he drops in a quote that’s surprisingly profound for him, and the twist is it’s actually Keanu Reeves who said it. We then looked at other Keanu Reeves quotes, and [we realized] he says quite a lot of profound things, so we were spoiled for choice. ( Laughs. ) “The simple act of paying attention can take you a long way” can apply to the technical preparations of a legal case. But I think [the quote] being so important and it being Keanu was just a great worlds colliding [moment] because Keanu Reeves is not something you’d [expect to] reference in this show about fusty British law firms, so it felt fun to us. Were you always planning for Johnny to be outed as the mole? Did you consider having him exposed earlier or later in the show? Did you ever consider letting him get away with it? We always felt he would be revealed at some point, and the most exciting point to reveal something is just at the moment you don’t need to reveal it for the case of the other characters. China Moo-Young, who directed the middle block — her final shot is the court doors closing on Johnny [after his slip-up], and the final act directed by Jen Sheridan is all in the court. So the idea that the second before the court case starts, all the other characters realize, “Hang on a sec. This is all completely compromised by the fact that we know who the mole is and he works for us,” felt like the hinge we wanted to create in the storyline. That was quite clear to us, but I think there were layers of drama to find behind that. So the idea that there might be a mole warrants a whole episode. The idea that that mole then tries to obfuscate who it is and come up with theories about his friends being moles or throw other people under the bus for his own survival becomes an episode. We really enjoyed peeling that onion and stretching him out over three episodes. There’s the Ferrari twist [in episode five, where a stray mention of a Ferrari Testarossa on an asset disclosure list exposes that there’s a mole inside Taylor & Byrne in the first place]. There’s a bit like an episode of Traitors , and then there’s the final rumbling on him based on this silly quote that capsizes the whole thing. Johnny spends the last two episodes of the season very much trying to atone and apologize for his mistakes while also fighting desperately for his own professional survival. Where did you want to leave him by the end of the season? I wanted him to have a nice attempt to salvage his situation, and I think we do root for him and we do want him to succeed — or at least I did. I don’t know how you felt. I could empathize with Johnny. I don’t necessarily agree with his choices, but I can see how his ambitions ultimately clouded his judgment. As a law student myself, I recognize some of my own classmates and future colleagues in him. Also, it’s a tightrope act; once you’re up there, you’ve got to do what you need to stay up there. Okay, he tries to salvage it all, he grows a heart, and he becomes morally a bit more aware — but not before he’s tried to switch sides back to Cathcarts. It’s just a desperate game of survival for a kid that has been exploitative himself, but also has been exploited by the system. When we talked about Johnny at the very beginning of this process, Ben Taylor, our brilliant [first] director, and I were looking at a lot of early ’90s Tom Cruise films, like The Firm . All those kinds of Tom Cruise characters felt like they were likable — you rooted for them, but they could sometimes overstep; they’re a bit too keen, a bit too ambitious. That’s what we wanted to tread with Johnny. It’s that thing of, “Oh my God, I know a guy like that. I don’t dislike him, but he’s really chancing his arm here. In a way, given everything he’s been through, I kind of hope he sticks to the landing.” Can you confirm that Johnny will be back for season two? He will be back for season two. We scoured London to find our Johnny Warren, and when Archie appeared, it was pretty clear to us that he was our guy. It’s a big ensemble show, so Johnny’s definitely a part of season two, and he’s got to pay for some of his decisions in season one. But also coming into the foreground [next season at Taylor & Byrne], we have Emma Laird, who plays Molly, and Nick Mohammed [who plays Michael] — they came into the show knowing they were going to have a big season two. We were making promises to them at the casting stage saying, “Listen, if you come into this ensemble show, your story will come to the fore in the second season.” We were already planning that when we were casting those actors for season one. That’s the real benefit of HBO and Sky backing us for a two-season order. We can start to layer in things, like the place where they buy their coffee from in season one — you see the cups with the logo on them — becomes a story point in season two. And in season two, they don’t talk on X; they talk on [Morgan’s social media platform] Zephyr. We continue the consistency of the world-building across the show, so it becomes a hermetically sealed thing. Whereas the first season centered on a messy, high-profile divorce, the second will focus on a defamation suit. In success, will each season of War focus on a different kind of legal dispute? Yes, totally. Dominic West in War . Will Cathcarts and Taylor & Byrne be representing the litigants in each case? The show’s built to be Cathcarts vs. Taylor & Byrne every season, and every season we’re going to have guest-star casting. So you have Dominic West divorcing Sienna Miller in season one. We have Marisa Tomei suing Kelly MacDonald for defamation in season two. [Marisa’s character, Avery Reed] flies over from London to claim damages for something that Jo MacNeil, Kelly’s character, has said. Of course, it means that the law firms have to pivot and bring their defamation lawyers to the fore, so there’s new casting to help with that. The more it goes on, it’ll be an anthology show where different guest-star clients will come in and occupy the space for Cathcarts and Taylor & Byrne, and we come up with organic, believable ways that those firms come up against each other once again. But all the while, you’re just building on what I think of as a fantastic ensemble British cast. So, hopefully, you’re coming back to the show just as much for Phoebe Fox and Nina Sosanya [who plays Beatrice] as you are for the next guest stars that are going to appear. Beyond the two-season order you were given, do you have a long-term plan for the series? Do you have a target number of seasons in mind? I just want to keep the show going with amazing guest stars and be able to nurture those characters on both sides of Cathcarts and Taylor & Byrne over subsequent seasons. It’s always been designed to come back three, four seasons more. I’m not intending to find an ending to it. I want to keep expanding and developing that ensemble cast. So there should be all number of cases we can do to keep pushing those characters into more and more dramatic situations. Johnny will certainly need to do a lot of work to get back in the good graces of Serena and Nick (James McArdle), who are last seen leaving the firm for Serena to give birth to their first child. What new layers of that relationship — and the rival firms — will you be exploring next season? One of the great fun questions we had as writers was, “Could you work with your partner?” We may not have been lawyers or divorced, but we could all answer that question, and we all had very different views. [Serena and Nick] are still together and they are parents in season two. It starts three months after the end of season one. Of course, Serena is no longer working day-to-day; she’s on maternity leave. Maybe the harder thing than working with your partner is working with your partner when you are not there to see what they’re doing. So it means there’s even more friendly, loving rivalry between them as they try and work out how to manage a law firm when one of them is staying at home all day. It’s been great to work with Phoebe because she was pregnant for real throughout season one, so then her maternity leave was real in season two. We do see Nick taking the lead a little bit more at the beginning of the season, if only because Phoebe Fox is on real maternity leave. ( Laughs .) Also, we go home with the lawyers from Taylor & Byrne a lot more in season one, and it was always designed that in season two, we would emphasize the home lives of Cathcarts. You get to know why the really harsh lawyers are so harsh — and they’re not just born harsh; they have to be turned that way by life. You get to go home with them and understand who they really are as humans a lot more. So with Pip [Torrens, who plays St. John] and Nina, you’ll see much more of their [characters’] home lives. In the finale, Johnny tells Flora that he thinks it’s impossible to be a good lawyer and a good person. He shares the cynical view that lawyers — especially those working in family litigation — are only ever acting in their own best interests. I wouldn’t want your characters to speak for you, but after having made this show, how do you feel about lawyers? It’s interesting because I have no more affection or dislike for lawyers than I do for any other walk of life. ( Laughs .) It’s all about different characters. I think the Johnny is more, “Is it possible [to be both]?” That’s the conundrum he faces, and for a character that’s going into the world of law and has been exposed to the dark tactics that are used in our show anyway, that question should come up. But I think the answer to that question is yes. I think Johnny’s not all bad. It’s been interesting to see how the audience has over the series moved around on Johnny, who has a great likability but still does things that people object to and objectively are hard to love. We had a brilliant consultant, Catherine Bedford. She’s a really impressive woman and was very helpful to us, and then [we’d] hear about other family lawyers who can be awful to people. So you want to retain a bit of self-deprecation among the lawyers. They’ve got to do terrible things, but they’ve got to be aware of it; they’ve got to have that self-awareness. So I think that they know when they’re being bad, and that makes them more interesting than if they just were doing bad stuff. *** All episodes of War are now streaming on HBO Max in the U.S. and Sky NOW in the U.K. THR

title: Sofia Coppola Pays Tribute to Late Mother Eleanor Coppola at Chanel-Hosted Paris Screening of ‘Making Marie Antoinette’
full_text: × Nov 20, 2026 7:38am PT Sofia Coppola Pays Tribute to Late Mother Eleanor Coppola at Chanel-Hosted Paris Screening of ‘Making Marie Antoinette’ By Elsa Keslassy Plus Icon Elsa Keslassy International Correspondent @elsakeslassy Latest Sofia Coppola Pays Tribute to Late Mother Eleanor Coppola at Chanel-Hosted Paris Screening of ‘Making Marie Antoinette’ 2 hours ago Bond Girl Lea Seydoux Says ‘I Don’t Really Care’ Who Becomes 007’s New Female Lead: ‘It’s Become American’ Now 24 hours ago Penelope Cruz to Star in and Produce Netflix Drama ‘Patricia’ From ‘On the Fringes’ Director Juan Diego Botto 1 day ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Sofia Coppola / Courtesy of Obscured Pictures Sofia Coppola paid tribute to her late mother, Eleanor Coppola, at the Paris premiere of the documentary “Making Marie Antoinette,” which she directed, charting the making of her daughter’s 2006 cult film starring Kirsten Dunst. While she was unable to attend after coming down with the flu, Coppola sent a heartfelt note honoring her mother, who “taught (her) so much, especially how to look for and see beauty around you.” Related Stories Jennifer Lopez on the ‘JLo Show’ Concert Film, Her ‘Happy Era’ and Moving on From Divorce: 'What I Thought Love Was Really Isn’t Love’ Elizabeth Debicki Says 'Tenet' Co-Star Robert Pattinson Will Be the ‘Perfect’ James Bond: ‘I’m So Thrilled’ The letter was read by producer Lorenzo Mieli at the special screening, which was hosted by Chanel and Mubi at the newly restored Le Saint-Germain-des-Prés cinema in Paris and marked the 20th anniversary of “Marie Antoinette.” Cannes Film Festival chief Thierry Frémaux was also on hand to introduce the documentary and reminisced about selecting “Marie Antoinette” for the festival in 2006. Frémaux recalled being immediately struck by how bold and distinctive Coppola’s take on the French queen was, and feeling that the film belonged in the festival’s official competition. The documentary, which world-premiered at Telluride and has been streaming on Mubi since Nov. 6, draws on footage shot by Eleanor Coppola during the epic production of “Marie Antoinette,” capturing her daughter’s creative process, as well as moments of doubt, intimate moments with Dunst and Schwartzman, sprawling rehearsal scenes, and shedding light on the craftsmanship behind the film’s elaborate costumes, sets and decor. “Making Marie Antoinette” also offers a glimpse of the Coppola family at work, with Sofia’s brother Roman Coppola directing second-unit footage and her father, Francis Ford Coppola, dropping by the set to offer advice. “My mom shot 80 hours of footage on the set of Marie Antoinette twenty years ago, and it was never put together the way she imagined. During lockdown we went through the footage and started to think about how it would take shape,” Coppola wrote. “On that set, my mom took great pleasure in recording all the detail that went into the making of the film – the costumes, Milena’s artistry, KK’s production design, the exquisitely elaborate food, flowers and decor.” “Having her on set meant there was a behind the scenes crew I didn’t feel self conscious in front of and nice to have my mom there during a challenging production. It was a surprise watching the footage for the first time with her, including her meeting my husband, Thomas, for the first time on camera,” Coppola continued. Eleanor Coppola, who died in April 2024 at age 87, was an acclaimed documentary filmmaker best known for “Hearts of Darkness: A Filmmaker’s Apocalypse,” which chronicled the notoriously troubled production of Francis Ford Coppola’s “Apocalypse Now.” In its review out of Telluride, Variety described “Making Marie Antoinette” as “lush, intimate and compulsively watchable,” praising Eleanor Coppola’s affectionate portrait of her daughter and the creative process behind the film. The review also highlighted a poignant moment in which Eleanor recalls a young Sofia pretending to direct on the set of her father’s “Apocalypse Now,” before growing up to direct her own period epic and carve out a place for herself in the still largely male-dominated film industry. “My daughter is directing it with clarity, grace, and her own hip approach to history,” Eleanor wrote in her diary, as quoted in Variety’s review. The screening was supported by Chanel, which has maintained a longstanding creative relationship with Sofia Coppola, a house ambassador. The French luxury brand previously designed the wedding dress worn by Cailee Spaeny in Coppola’s 2023 film “Priscilla” and has supported filmmaking documentaries including “Room 999” and Richard Linklater’s “Nouvelle Vague.” “Making Marie Antoinette” is produced by Sofia Coppola, Mieli, Mario Gianani, Rachel Dengiz and Youree Henley for Our Films, a Mediawan company, and American Zoetrope. The documentary is financed by Our Films, Mediawan Rights and Entourage Media. title: Robert Pattinson’s Bond Ascent: How Pricey Screen Tests and Amazon Execs Landed a Starry 007
full_text: × Nov 20, 2026 7:35am PT Robert Pattinson’s Bond Ascent: How Pricey Screen Tests and Amazon Execs Landed a Starry 007 By Matt Donnelly Plus Icon Matt Donnelly Chief Correspondent @MattDonnelly Latest Shop of Horrors: How Talent Representation Firm Verve Became Hollywood’s Home for Successful Scares 1 week ago Industry Trio Launch Distinkt, AI-Powered Agency for Global Talent (EXCLUSIVE) 1 week ago Skydance Succession: As David Ellison Sets His Team, Heads Are Rolling as Hollywood Finds Out Who’s Really in Charge 1 week ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Amazon MGM What does an actor do in the quiet moments before the announcement that will change his life? For Robert Pattinson , there were about 12 hours between the Sunday phone call confirming he’d landed the role of James Bond and Amazon MGM’s Monday-morning release of the first image of the actor rocking a tuxedo and pistol. He spent it, rather predictably, watching an arthouse horror film. Related Stories ‘La Bola Negra’ to Receive International Star Award at Palm Springs International Film Festival (EXCLUSIVE) Gemma Chan Says She’d ‘Absolutely’ Play a Bond Girl Amid Fan-Casting: ‘I’m Flattered’ His longtime friend and collaborator Robert Eggers told Variety this week that Pattinson was screening the director’s forthcoming genre drama “Werwulf” when the Bond news broke. Nothing like a stark naked Aaron Taylor-Johnson terrorizing a quaint village to pass the time. But after months (years, really) of toiling and speculation over who would replace Daniel Craig in the film adaptations of Ian Fleming’s spy novels, Pattinson took the crown. It buttons up a delicious, messy and very public guessing game over which lucky man would land the iconic role. When Amazon MGM bought out rights to James Bond from longtime custodians the Broccoli family in 2025, intentions were set for a young star who could shoulder the franchise for a decade or two. An A-list team of producers (Amy Pascal of “Spider-Man” and David Heyman of the “Harry Potter” movies) recruited Denis Villeneuve to direct. Together, with significant influence from Amazon execs Courtenay Valenti and Mike Hopkins (and yes, Jeff Bezos), they screen-tested a laundry list of virile performers — including Callum Turner, Tom Francis, Jack Lowden and Josh O’Connor — earlier this year. For the curious, the batch of screen tests cost Amazon MGM between $300,000 and $500,000 to pull off, ostensibly in secret (everyone found out), sources familiar with the process say. But two wildcard actors who tested at the last minute — “Superman” star Nicholas Hoult and the DCU’s reining Batman, Pattinson — tipped the scales. Villeneuve’s voice became the most trusted in the room on the matter of Bond’s casting, two insiders tell Variety . His shorthand with Pattinson from working on “Dune: Part Three” made the choice inevitable, according to industry insiders — especially after Turner, the early favorite, came under scrutiny against more established names like Hoult and Pattinson. Lowden, the heat-seeking star of “Slow Horses,” was even the subject of a suspected sabotage campaign when paparazzi footage circulated showed the actor bungling an on-set motorcycle stunt just two weeks before the Bond casting was confirmed. A sect of the internet lost its mind when Variety reported earlier this month that Harry Styles and Theo James were both in talks for the role. It’s rare, even by tentpole movie standards, that such a long list of candidates would flow so freely through public channels. The studios hate it because it makes them seem indecisive, one exec says. Talent absolutely hates it because the also-rans will have to answer for almost being James Bond on talk show couches and podcasts for the next 10 years. “Whatever, it’s really fun,” one top talent rep tells Variety of the audition merry-go-round. While there will be detractors, it’s inarguable that the Bond gig now enshrines Pattinson in the upper echelons of movie stardom. He was already well on his way, with even civilian social media pundits having commented on the “generational run” Pattinson has been living out onscreen in films like “Primetime,” “The Odyssey,” “The Drama,” “Die My Love” and, obviously, “The Batman.” That’s to say nothing of the deeply indie era (“Good Time,” “The Lighthouse”) that followed major franchise moments like his star-making turn in the “Twilight Saga” movies and a prominent role in “Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire.” The new job also represents a major win for Pattinson’s agent of more than 20 years, Stephanie Ritz of WME. Ritz and team have managed to populate massive IP with Pattinson’s face while still allowing the actor to take risks and brand himself a maverick for the cross-generational devotees of studios like A24. Given the shocking November news that DC Studios heads James Gunn and Peter Safran had been jettisoned by the David Ellison regime, it’s doubtful Pattinson would linger long as Matt Reeves’ caped crusader — freeing him up to embody the sultry British charm and execute the bare-knuckle action audiences have come to expect from 007. Art-house horror movies may have to take a back seat. title: Prince Harry Approves of Robert Pattinson’s Bond Casting
full_text: × Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All November 20, 2026 7:27am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Prince Harry (left) and our first look at Pattinson's James Bond. Courtesy of Getty/Jaap Buitendijk Prince Harry made a surprise appearance on British daytime television on Friday, where he gave incoming 007 Robert Pattinson the royal seal of approval. In his first appearance on ITV’s This Morning since moving back to the U.K., the Duke of Sussex was asked about Monday’s news that Pattinson has been tapped to succeed Daniel Craig as James Bond in the new film from Amazon MGM Studios . “I think it’s great,” said Harry to hosts Alison Hammond and Dermot O’Leary about the casting news. “I can’t wait to see it.” When asked to choose between Tom Cruise’s Mission Impossible franchise or the MI6 agent, the royal made his allegiance clear. “James Bond, 100 per cent, [and] I want to make sure that is in good hands.” Related Stories Business Andrea Scrosati to Leave Fremantle Group Music 'Adolescence' Breakout Owen Cooper Leads New Music Video for Beatles Hit 'In My Life' Amazon bought the creative rights to the Bond franchise from producer siblings Michael G. Wilson and Barbara Broccoli last year and blew up the internet by releasing Pattinson’s casting via 007’s official social media accounts. Harry’s father and stepmother, King Charles and Queen Camilla, immediately quoted the post and welcomed The Batman , The Odyssey and Primetime star into the fold. Their account wrote on Monday: “Welcome to His Majesty’s Secret Service, Mr Bond.” Pattinson won a months-long race for the role , beating fellow screen-testers Callum Turner, Josh O’Connor and Jack Lowden. Villeneuve, who recently worked with Pattinson on the final Dune outing, is directing a script from Peaky Blinders mastermind Steven Knight. The current timeline suggests a 2028 release. In a development that shocked Britain, Harry and wife Meghan Markle moved from California back to the U.K. — around the Cotswolds area — in August, where they enrolled 7-year-old Prince Archie and 5-year-old Princess Lilibet in school. The Duke joked on This Morning that he is slowly “squeezing” the American accents out of his children. He also talked about being a huge Great British Bake Off fan and revealed that Markle and his mother-in-law will be doing the brunt of the Christmas cooking over the holiday period. Harry and Meghan have begun to make more public appearances here since moving back, even though King Charles maintains that they remain private citizens and are not working royal family members. Markle’s estranged father, Thomas Markle Sr., has grabbed headlines in recent weeks for being at the center of an alleged police probe into child abuse imagery. “I am deeply distressed at the news,” said the Duchess in a public statement in October. “[I hope] it can now be understood, that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them.” THR

title: Andrea Scrosati to Leave Fremantle Group
full_text: × Skip to main content By Scott Roxborough Plus Icon Scott Roxborough Europe Bureau Chief sroxborough Follow Sign Up View All November 20, 2026 7:07am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Andrea Scrosati, Fremantle’s group COO and CEO Continental Europe Fremantle Fremantle Group COO and CEO Continental Europe Andrea Scrosati is stepping down after an eight-year tenure in which he oversaw an ambitious expansion of the Fremantle’s international production operations, including the acquisition of multiple independent film and TV production companies. Fremantle announced Friday that Scrosati, who joined the company from Sky Italia in 2018, and was named CEO Continental Europe in 2021, is stepping down to pursue a new entrepreneurial venture. He will stay on until the end of January 2027 to support the transition to new leadership. During his tenure, Scrosati led Fremantle’s mergers and acquisitions strategy, transforming the company from a business primarily associated with international entertainment formats into a global production group with a substantial presence in premium drama, independent film and documentaries. Among the most significant acquisitions included Dublin-based Element Pictures, the production company behind The Favourite , Room and Normal People ; Italian producer Lux Vide, whose credits include Medici , Leonardo and Devils ; and the Asacha Media Group, which owns eight production labels across France, Italy, including Red Planet Pictures, the British producer of Death in Paradise , and Italy’s Picomedia. The acquisitions also provided the foundation for Fremantle’s expansion in film. Among the major productions backed during Scrosati’s tenure were Yorgos Lanthimos’ Poor Things ; Joanna Hogg’s The Eternal Daughter ; Ali Abbasi’s The Apprentice ; and Sebastián Lelio’s The Wonder . During Scrosati’s tenure, Fremantle racked up 17 Oscar nominations and four Academy Awards for its titles. Scrosati also oversaw Fremantle’s expansion into documentaries and sports programing, the growth of its free ad-supported streaming television (FAST) channel business and the creation of Imaginae Studios, a standalone production label focused on artificial intelligence. Its first production, Art Awakens , launched in 2026. The M&A activity was part of a broader growth strategy set by Fremantle’s parent company RTL Group, which in 2021 set an ambitious target of doubling Fremantle’s annual revenue to €3 billion ($3.3 billion) within four years, through acquisitions and the expansion of Fremantle’s production businesses. The company did not reach that goal. Revenue peaked at approximately €2.27 billion in 2023 before falling to €2.254 billion in 2024 and €2.043 billion in 2025, leaving it nearly €1 billion short of the original target. RTL has subsequently pushed the €3 billion ambition further into the future. “Andrea has made an enormous contribution to Fremantle over the past eight years,” Jennifer Mullin, Global CEO Fremantle, said in a statement. “He has been instrumental in our growth and transformation, from helping build Fremantle into a true portfolio company and leading our M&A strategy, to establishing our film strategy and constantly pushing us to think differently about innovation and the future of our business.” Scrosati said the time was right to move on and focus on building something new. “I leave with enormous pride in what we have achieved together and great affection for the company and everyone who makes it what it is.” THR

Daisy Ridley ( Ebenezer ), Darren Criss ( Glee ), Travis Fimmel ( Dune: Prophecy ) and Judy Greer ( Ant-Man ) have joined Catherine Zeta-Jones in Tate Taylor’s psychological thriller Cupid , which is now filming in Natchez, Mississippi. Tate Taylor ( The Girl On The Train ) is directing from a screenplay by the Van Dyke brothers ( Don’t Worry Darling ). Cupid “follows a couple (Ridley and Criss) whose relationship is on the rocks as they try, over one weekend, to repair their marriage at the home of a seemingly helpful but unorthodox marriage counselor (Zeta-Jones). What starts out as a hopeful endeavor quickly turns dark as her methods become crueler and more dangerous.” Taylor and John Norris are producing alongside Ryan Donnell Smith. Watch on Deadline Upgrade is handling international sales and CAA Media Finance, which arranged financing for the film, is handling U.S. distribution rights. Sales discussions continue at the AFM . Ridley is represented by CAA and Sloane, Offer; Criss is represented by Gersh, Hyphenate Creative, Gersh, and Hansen, Jacobson; Fimmel is represented by Paradigm, Entertainment 360, & Sloane Offer; and Greer is represented by CAA, Artists First, and Felker Toczek.
